**Proof.**

Yes, it is necessarily true that $\|u\|_X = 0$.

We prove the contrapositive: if $\|u\|_X > 0$, then there exists $f \in X^*$ with $\langle f, u \rangle \neq 0$.

Assume $u \neq 0$, i.e., $\|u\|_X > 0$. Consider the one-dimensional subspace $Y = \operatorname{span}\{u\} \subseteq X$. Define a linear functional $g : Y \to \mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{C}$) by
$$g(\alpha u) = \alpha \|u\|_X.$$
Then $g$ is a bounded linear functional on $Y$ with $\|g\|_{Y^*} = 1$, since
$$|g(\alpha u)| = |\alpha|\,\|u\|_X = \|\alpha u\|_Y,$$
so $|g(y)| = \|y\|$ for all $y \in Y$, giving $\|g\| = 1$.

By the **Hahn–Banach theorem**, $g$ extends to a bounded linear functional $f \in X^*$ with $\|f\|_{X^*} = \|g\|_{Y^*} = 1$. In particular,
$$\langle f, u \rangle = g(u) = \|u\|_X > 0.$$

This contradicts the hypothesis that $\langle f, u \rangle = 0$ for all $f \in X^*$. Therefore $u = 0$, i.e., $\|u\|_X = 0$.

**Remark.** This is the standard corollary of Hahn–Banach asserting that $X^*$ separates points of $X$: the canonical embedding $J : X \to X^{**}$, defined by $J(u)(f) = \langle f, u \rangle$, is an isometry. Hence $J(u) = 0$ implies $\|u\|_X = \|J(u)\|_{X^{**}} = 0$.
